title: Debt service is becoming a public-capacity and everyday-development constraint, especially in developing economies
source_unit: UNCTAD A World of Debt 2025, global and developing-country public-debt analysis
geography: Global public debt and developing-country comparisons; the report's country counts and regional shares follow UNCTAD's debt datasets

observations.period: 2024 public-debt stock and interest-payment indicators; report published 26 June 2025

denominator.unit: US dollars of global public debt in 2024

global_public_debt.unit: trillion US dollars in 2024, up from $97 trillion in 2023

developing_country_interest_payments.unit: billion US dollars in net public-debt interest payments in 2024, up 10% from 2023

countries_over_ten_percent_revenue_inter.unit: developing countries allocating at least 10% of government revenue to net interest payments in 2024

people_in_countries_interest_exceeds_hea.unit: people living in countries where interest payments exceed spending on either health or education

observations.method: UNCTAD synthesis of public-debt, interest-payment, government-revenue, and public-expenditure indicators, with regional and income-group comparisons and international-financial-architecture analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Debt and expenditure concepts use the report's definitions and may not be directly comparable across countries. Interest exceeding health or education spending is a country-level budget comparison, not proof that an individual lost a service or that debt alone caused a spending decision.
observations.subgroup: Developing countries, least-developed and vulnerable economies, national governments, creditors, public services, and populations exposed to constrained health, education, infrastructure, or climate spending.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public debt can finance productive investment and protect people; high interest burdens can coexist with effective service delivery. A high aggregate interest bill does not identify the quality, composition, or distribution of public spending.

denominator.unit: percent of developing-country comparison group for reported shares and ranges

borrowing_rate_multiple_us.unit: times US borrowing rates: average rates paid by developing regions since 2020

external_public_debt_service.unit: billion US dollars paid by developing countries to service external public debt in 2023

countries_at_least_6_5_percent_exports_e.unit: percent of developing countries spending at least 6.5% of export revenues on external public-debt service

negative_net_resource_transfer.unit: billion US dollars more paid to external creditors than received in fresh disbursements in 2023

international_finance_reform_route.value: inclusive governance, crisis liquidity, effective debt workouts, concessional finance, and technical assistance

observations.method: UNCTAD comparison of borrowing costs, external debt service, export-revenue exposure, fresh disbursements, and net resource transfers, linked to proposed reforms of the international financial architecture.
observations.uncertainty: The relative borrowing-cost comparison is an average across developing regions and does not describe every sovereign. Net transfers and debt-service measures are macro aggregates; they do not measure household incidence, default probability, or whether reform would improve a particular public programme.
observations.subgroup: Developing-country governments, exporters, public borrowers, creditors, multilateral institutions, and residents affected by fiscal trade-offs and external financing conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: External borrowing can support investment and countercyclical protection when terms and projects are sustainable. A negative net transfer in one year does not establish insolvency or rule out future development gains.

related_sources.claim: UNCTAD provides the official full A World of Debt 2025 report and source notes.
UNCTAD connects debt service to health, education, development financing, and public-capacity trade-offs.

boundary: This record adds a macro-finance-to-public-capacity route. It does not estimate household incidence, attribute service cuts to debt alone, evaluate a specific debt restructuring, or treat national debt totals as individual economic outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: UNCTAD A World of Debt 2025 publication page, official report materials, and official news summary retrieved; debt stocks, interest payments, public-revenue shares, population exposure, borrowing-cost comparison, external debt service, resource transfer, and reform pathways cross-checked against UNCTAD materials.
